title: JWT & OAuth
objectives: Read a JWT's three parts and know what the signature protects
Explain the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
Distinguish access, refresh and ID tokens

sections.markdown: A **JWT** is a signed token with three Base64URL parts: header.payload.signature. **OAuth 2.0** lets a user grant a third-party app scoped access without sharing their password.
JWT payloads are Base64-encoded, **not encrypted** — anyone can read them. Never put passwords/secrets in a JWT. The signature only proves it wasn't tampered with.
Accepting alg:'none' or letting the client choose the algorithm lets attackers forge tokens. Always pin the expected algorithm server-side.

sections.code:
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow:
  User clicks 'Login' -> redirected to Auth Server (Google)
  User approves consent -> redirect back with CODE
  App exchanges code + secret -> access token + refresh token
  App calls API with the access token

sections.markdown: Use Authorization Code + **PKCE** for mobile/SPA apps (the Implicit flow is deprecated). Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens get new ones without re-login.

flashcards.back: No — it's Base64-encoded and signed. Anyone can read the payload; the signature only prevents tampering.
Access token is short-lived and sent on each API call; refresh token is long-lived and used to get new access tokens.

quiz.q: What does a JWT signature guarantee?
quiz.explain: The signature ensures integrity, not confidentiality — the payload is readable.

quiz.q: In OAuth 2.0, what is exchanged for tokens?
quiz.explain: The app exchanges the short-lived authorization code (with its secret) for tokens.

quiz.q: Which flow should a mobile app use?
quiz.explain: PKCE protects the code exchange on public clients; Implicit is deprecated.
